subtopic_detail: Haemodynamic instability with echocardiographic RV strain
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED reviewing a 58-year-old man with sudden dyspnoea and collapse 2 days after a long haul flight from Los Angeles. He has a heart rate of 132, blood pressure 82/48 despite 2 litres of crystalloid, and cool peripheries. Oxygen saturation is 88 percent on 15 litres via non-rebreather. Bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with paradoxical septal motion. CT pulmonary angiogram confirms bilateral saddle embolus. He is on no anticoagulant and has no bleeding contraindications.

The intensivist has intubation prepared and asks about definitive reperfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 92 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 480 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: CTPA bilateral saddle embolus with RV/LV ratio 1.6, bedside echo dilated hypokinetic RV

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Catheter directed thrombolysis with reduced dose alteplase 24 mg over 12 hours plus IV heparin infusion
options.rationale: Catheter directed thrombolysis is considered for submassive PE where bleeding risk from full dose systemic tPA is high; in massive PE with shock, systemic tPA is faster and first line. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kg twice daily alone with careful volume replacement and inotrope support
options.rationale: Anticoagulation alone does not reperfuse and is insufficient in massive PE with obstructive shock; reperfusion by thrombolysis or embolectomy is required. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Immediate surgical embolectomy on cardiopulmonary bypass without first attempting systemic thrombolysis
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is second line if thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated; first line for massive PE without contraindication is systemic tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Systemic alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion targeted to APTT
options.rationale: Massive PE with sustained hypotension and RV dysfunction is a class I indication for systemic thrombolysis with alteplase; concurrent unfractionated heparin is titrated to APTT after tPA. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

options.text: Insert an IVC filter first, then start therapeutic heparin infusion and reassess for tPA at 24 hours
options.rationale: IVC filters do not treat the existing clot causing shock and delaying tPA is dangerous in massive PE; filters are reserved for anticoagulation contraindication or recurrence on therapy. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

explanation.summary: Massive (high risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension or shock from acute PE. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus concurrent unfractionated heparin is first line when there are no absolute bleeding contraindications. Surgical embolectomy or catheter directed thrombolysis are reserved for failed or contraindicated systemic tPA. Anticoagulation alone or IVC filter placement do not treat the obstruction.
key_points: Massive PE: shock or hypotension plus PE, immediate reperfusion needed
Alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours plus UFH infusion is first line
Surgical embolectomy or CDT if tPA fails or contraindicated
IVC filter only when anticoagulation is contraindicated
explanation.pearls: PE mortality with shock is around 30 to 50 percent untreated and falls to 10 to 20 percent with prompt tPA; alteplase 0.6 mg per kg over 15 minutes bolus is used in cardiac arrest from suspected PE, standard 100 mg over 2 hours in sustained shock without arrest.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology PE Statement

subtopic_detail: pH 6.90 with severe hypokalaemia and altered conscious level
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 24-year-old woman with new type 1 diabetes presenting with 24 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13. She is Kussmaul breathing at 32 per minute. Blood pressure is 96/58 with pulse 128. Weight is 60 kg. Venous blood gas pH is 6.90 with a bicarbonate of 4 and anion gap of 34. Plasma glucose is 32 mmol/L, potassium is 3.0, and creatinine 132. She has no urinary ketone strip but capillary ketones are 6.8.

Her initial 500 mL crystalloid bolus is running. You must set the initial insulin and potassium plan.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 4 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 132 umol/L (45-90), glucose 32 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), pH 6.90, ketones 6.8 mmol/L (under 0.6), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (under 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start dextrose 10 percent infusion and normal insulin infusion together to avoid rapid glucose fall over 2 hours
options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin, not initially at glucose 32; and insulin cannot start until K over 3.3 mmol/L is corrected. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Start fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour immediately alongside crystalloid resuscitation
options.rationale: Starting insulin with potassium under 3.3 mmol/L causes dangerous intracellular potassium shift and arrhythmia; correct K to 3.5 first. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 30 minutes because pH is under 7.00 with cardiovascular risk
options.rationale: Bicarbonate does not improve outcomes in DKA and can worsen hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema risk; it is not routinely indicated even at pH under 7.00 unless refractory shock is present. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give a subcutaneous rapid acting insulin bolus of 10 units and then commence oral fluids and delay IV insulin
options.rationale: SC insulin is unreliable in shock or dehydration and is not first line in severe DKA; IV infusion is standard, and hypokalaemia must be corrected before starting insulin. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Continue crystalloid resuscitation and replace potassium to over 3.5 mmol/L before starting insulin infusion
options.rationale: Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives further intracellular shift and precipitates arrhythmia; correct K first, then start insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour. (Source: ADS DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe DKA with initial potassium under 3.3 mmol/L is a contraindication to starting insulin because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and precipitates arrhythmia. The priority is fluid resuscitation and potassium replacement to above 3.5 mmol/L before commencing IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units per kg per hour. Bicarbonate is not routine even at pH under 7.00. Add dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin infusion.
key_points: Potassium under 3.3 mmol/L: hold insulin until corrected to above 3.5
Standard fixed rate insulin: 0.1 units per kg per hour IV
Bicarbonate not routinely indicated in DKA even at pH under 7.00
Add dextrose 10 percent when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L on insulin
explanation.pearls: ADS thresholds: hold insulin K under 3.3, add KCl 40 mmol per litre if K 3.3 to 5.3; cerebral oedema risk in adults is low but reduce fluid rate if child, symptoms occur usually 4 to 12 hours in, treat with mannitol 0.5 to 1 g per kg or 3 percent saline 5 mL per kg.

subtopic_detail: M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion at 4 hours from onset
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a metropolitan ED reviewing a 68-year-old right-handed man who developed sudden left hemiparesis and neglect 4 hours ago on a family car trip. NIHSS is 18 with dense left arm weakness, forced right gaze deviation, and hemispatial neglect. He is on aspirin 100 mg for coronary disease. Non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage and no established infarct; ASPECTS is 9. CT angiogram confirms a right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion shows a mismatch ratio of 2.1 with core 18 mL and penumbra 58 mL. He has no thrombolysis contraindications and weighs 82 kg.

Interventional neuroradiology is available in-house.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 86, blood pressure 168/94, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, GCS 14
data_table.Bloods: Hb 148 g/L (135-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 umol/L (60-110), INR 1.0, glucose 6.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0)
data_table.Imaging: NCCT ASPECTS 9 no bleed, CTA right M1 occlusion, CTP core 18 mL penumbra 58 mL mismatch 2.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg bolus now followed by endovascular thrombectomy for the M1 occlusion
options.rationale: Within 4.5 hours of onset with no contraindication, IV thrombolysis (tenecteplase or alteplase) plus endovascular thrombectomy for a large vessel occlusion is first line and outperforms either alone. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Endovascular thrombectomy alone without IV thrombolysis because he is on aspirin already
options.rationale: Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis; skipping tPA loses the benefit of pre-thrombectomy reperfusion and small vessel clot clearance. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: IV thrombolysis only without thrombectomy because the CT ASPECTS score is 9 and core is small
options.rationale: Large vessel occlusion with disabling deficit benefits from thrombectomy even after tPA; withholding it wastes proven mortality and functional benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Loading dose clopidogrel 300 mg plus aspirin 300 mg and admit to the stroke unit without reperfusion
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet loading is not reperfusion and is not appropriate as sole therapy in disabling stroke with LVO within the reperfusion window. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

options.text: Delay reperfusion until 24 hours to allow perfusion imaging repeat and reduce haemorrhagic transformation risk
options.rationale: Delay of reperfusion loses time-dependent benefit; the mismatch profile at 4 hours already supports urgent tPA plus thrombectomy. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines Australia)

explanation.summary: Acute ischaemic stroke with a disabling deficit and confirmed anterior circulation large vessel occlusion should receive IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours if no contraindication, plus endovascular thrombectomy up to 24 hours with favourable imaging. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg has non-inferior evidence to alteplase and is now often first line in Australia. Combined therapy is better than either alone.
key_points: IV tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg within 4.5 hours of onset for eligible patients
Endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 24 hours with mismatch
Antiplatelet use is not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis
Blood pressure target under 185/110 before tPA, under 180/105 for 24 hours after
explanation.pearls: Australian Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines now recommend tenecteplase 0.25 mg per kg IV single bolus as an alternative to alteplase within 4.5 hours; thrombectomy has NNT around 4 to 5 for functional independence in LVO stroke within 6 hours.

subtopic_detail: Anterior STEMI with pulmonary oedema and hypotension after primary PCI
stem:
You are the coronary care unit registrar 4 hours after successful primary PCI to the LAD in a 62-year-old man with anterior STEMI. He is now hypotensive with blood pressure 78/52 despite noradrenaline at 0.4 mcg per kg per minute. He has bibasal crackles, JVP raised to angle, and cool peripheries. Echocardiogram shows LV ejection fraction 20 percent with anterior akinesis, moderate mitral regurgitation, and no mechanical complication. Lactate is 4.2. He is intubated and sedated. Cardiac output monitoring shows CI 1.6.

The interventional cardiologist has confirmed no residual coronary lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 78/52 on noradrenaline 0.4, respiratory rate 22 ventilated, SpO2 92% on 60% FiO2, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (135-175), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 138 umol/L (60-110), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (under 2.0), high sensitivity troponin 42000 ng/L (under 26)
data_table.Imaging: echo LVEF 20% anterior akinesis moderate MR no VSD no tamponade, chest X-ray bilateral alveolar oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in circulatory support?

options.text: Add dobutamine 5 mcg per kg per minute to noradrenaline and continue medical therapy with diuretics
options.rationale: Adding an inotrope on top of high dose vasopressor in worsening shock is unlikely to reverse hypoperfusion and delays escalation to mechanical support with proven benefit. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Insert an Impella CP percutaneous LV assist device and wean noradrenaline as cardiac output improves
options.rationale: In cardiogenic shock after STEMI unresponsive to inotropes with escalating lactate, mechanical circulatory support (Impella or VA-ECMO in some centres) is indicated; the DanGer Shock trial showed Impella CP mortality benefit in selected STEMI shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Give IV nitroglycerin infusion at 20 mcg per minute to reduce afterload and improve pulmonary oedema now
options.rationale: Nitroglycerin lowers preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in cardiogenic shock with SBP under 90; it is inappropriate as an escalation step here. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Give IV levosimendan 0.1 mcg per kg per minute over 24 hours and continue current vasopressor support
options.rationale: Levosimendan can worsen hypotension in fixed cardiogenic shock and has not shown mortality benefit; it is not the priority when mechanical support is available. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

options.text: Insert an intra-aortic balloon pump because IABP has proven mortality benefit in cardiogenic shock post-MI
options.rationale: IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI cardiogenic shock; contemporary practice favours Impella or VA-ECMO for refractory shock. (Source: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement)
source_refs: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

explanation.summary: Refractory cardiogenic shock after STEMI with escalating vasopressor need and rising lactate is an indication for mechanical circulatory support, with recent evidence (DanGer Shock 2024) supporting Impella CP over IABP or medical therapy alone in selected STEMI shock. IABP has no mortality benefit. Adding more inotropes or preload reducers can worsen outcomes. Early escalation before multi-organ failure is key.
key_points: Refractory STEMI cardiogenic shock: escalate to mechanical support early
DanGer Shock trial: Impella CP mortality benefit in STEMI shock
IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit for IABP in post-MI shock
Avoid vasodilators like GTN when SBP under 90 mmHg
explanation.pearls: DanGer Shock 2024 NEJM showed 6 month mortality 45.8 percent Impella CP vs 58.5 percent standard care in STEMI shock, at cost of more bleeding and limb ischaemia; VA-ECMO used when biventricular failure or Impella insufficient.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Cardiology STEMI Statement

subtopic_detail: Type 2 respiratory failure on maximal medical therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar in ED with a 26-year-old woman with severe asthma who has not improved after continuous nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, and IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes. She is diaphoretic, unable to speak in words, and has a silent chest. Peak flow was 90 L/min on arrival (best 420) and now cannot be recorded. Arterial gas 30 minutes into treatment shows pH 7.21, pCO2 68, pO2 62 on 15 L via non-rebreather. Heart rate is 148. She has a prior ICU admission for asthma.

The ICU consultant is at bedside for airway management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 132/86, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0), pH 7.21, pCO2 68 mmHg (35-45), pO2 62 mmHg (80-100)
data_table.Imaging: chest X-ray hyperinflation no pneumothorax no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV aminophylline 5 mg per kg loading dose over 20 minutes then continuous infusion 0.5 mg per kg per hour
options.rationale: Aminophylline has limited additional benefit over maximal beta-agonist plus magnesium and adds arrhythmia risk in a patient already needing intubation. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Continuous BiPAP 12/6 cmH2O with pressure support titration and repeat gas in 30 minutes before intubation
options.rationale: NIV in severe asthma with silent chest, exhaustion, and rising CO2 delays definitive airway and risks arrest; intubation is indicated now, not further NIV. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg per kg IV and rocuronium then lung protective ventilation
options.rationale: Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 and exhaustion after maximal therapy requires intubation; ketamine is preferred induction agent for bronchodilator effect and cardiovascular stability, with permissive hypercapnia thereafter. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: Repeat IV magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus and add second dose IV hydrocortisone before considering intubation
options.rationale: Repeating magnesium is not evidence supported and steroid effect takes hours; the patient needs an airway now, not another delayed pharmacological trial. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

options.text: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05 mcg per kg per minute and continue nebulised beta-agonist without airway plan
options.rationale: Systemic adrenaline is reserved for peri-arrest anaphylaxis or shock; it does not replace intubation in exhausted asthma with rising CO2 and silent chest. (Source: TSANZ/ANZSA Severe Asthma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe or near-fatal asthma with exhaustion, silent chest, and rising CO2 despite maximal medical therapy requires intubation. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent for its bronchodilator effect. Post-intubation ventilation uses low tidal volumes, low rate, long expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia to avoid dynamic hyperinflation. NIV is not first line in this deteriorating scenario.
key_points: Life threatening asthma with rising CO2 or silent chest: intubate
Ketamine 1 to 2 mg per kg IV is preferred induction agent
Permissive hypercapnia and prolonged expiratory time post intubation
Watch for dynamic hyperinflation and pneumothorax during ventilation
explanation.pearls: TSANZ suggests tidal volume 5 to 6 mL per kg, RR 8 to 10, I:E 1:4, plateau pressure under 30, allow pCO2 up to 80 mmHg with pH over 7.15; ketamine dose 1 to 2 mg per kg IV, with rocuronium 1.2 mg per kg for RSI.

subtopic_detail: Na 110 mmol/L with seizure and altered conscious state
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 74-year-old woman brought to ED after a witnessed 2 minute generalised seizure at home. She has been vomiting for 3 days and is on hydrochlorothiazide and citalopram. GCS is 12 now, no localising signs, no meningism. Sodium is 110, potassium 3.4, urea 6.4, creatinine 92, glucose 5.2. Serum osmolality is 240 and urine sodium 62. She is not clinically dehydrated. Airway is patent and BP is 122/74.

The intensivist is present and asks about immediate fluid strategy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, GCS 12
data_table.Bloods: sodium 110 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.4 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 92 umol/L (45-90), glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-8.0), serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L
data_table.Imaging: CT brain unremarkable, chest X-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate fluid management?

options.text: Give tolvaptan 15 mg orally now and start 0.9 percent saline at 100 mL per hour after loading dose is given
options.rationale: Tolvaptan risks over-rapid correction and osmotic demyelination and is not first line in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic saline in controlled boluses is standard. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Start 0.9 percent saline infusion at 500 mL per hour and reassess sodium in 4 hours before other action
options.rationale: Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatraemia by adding to intake in SIAD physiology; symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs hypertonic saline, not isotonic infusion, to raise sodium quickly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL per day and observe on the ward without giving any bolus of saline for 24 hours
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone is far too slow for a patient with active seizure and Na 110; hypertonic saline is needed to stop cerebral symptoms rapidly. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Give 150 mL 3 percent saline bolus IV over 10 minutes and repeat once or twice to a maximum rise of 6 mmol/L in 24 hours
options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is treated with hypertonic saline boluses to raise sodium by 4 to 6 mmol/L rapidly to stop symptoms, capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

options.text: Give IV frusemide 40 mg and 0.9 percent saline together to remove free water and raise sodium concentration
options.rationale: Frusemide plus isotonic saline can be used cautiously in some volume overload chronic cases but is inappropriate in acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; hypertonic bolus stops cerebral symptoms fastest. (Source: European Hyponatraemia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure or reduced GCS is treated with 150 mL 3 percent saline IV over 10 minutes, repeated once or twice, targeting a rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort cerebral symptoms, then capped at 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Isotonic saline can worsen the picture in SIAD-type physiology. Tolvaptan and free water restriction are for chronic settings.
key_points: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: 150 mL 3% saline bolus over 10 minutes
Repeat once or twice to raise Na 4 to 6 mmol/L to abort symptoms
Cap correction at 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent ODS
Do not use tolvaptan in acute symptomatic phase
explanation.pearls: European guideline (2014) and Aussie NKF: 150 mL 3% saline IV over 10 minutes as bolus; if over-correction occurs, give 5% dextrose 10 mL per kg over 1 hour plus DDAVP 2 to 4 mcg subcut to reverse.

subtopic_detail: Adult with subacute meningism and CSF lymphocytosis with low glucose
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 42-year-old man from a high TB prevalence country with 3 weeks of headache, fever, and progressive drowsiness. He has right sixth nerve palsy and mild neck stiffness. HIV serology is pending. CT brain shows basal meningeal enhancement and mild hydrocephalus with open ventricles. Lumbar puncture opening pressure is 32 cm CSF, protein 2.2 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L with paired plasma 6.4, and 240 lymphocytes with 20 neutrophils. GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive on CSF is available in 2 hours.

He is stable but drowsy. You must initiate treatment now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 124/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees Celsius, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (135-175), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 86 umol/L (60-110), ALT 32 U/L (5-40), CRP 68 mg/L (under 5)
data_table.Imaging: CT brain basal meningeal enhancement mild hydrocephalus, chest X-ray upper lobe infiltrates and small right hilar node

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start rifampicin and isoniazid only for 12 months with pyridoxine and defer pyrazinamide until sputum is available
options.rationale: Two-drug induction is inadequate for TB meningitis and risks resistance and treatment failure; standard four-drug induction with steroids is indicated even before sputum results. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV 4 hourly awaiting culture data
options.rationale: Bacterial meningitis cover alone misses TB, and the CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, high protein, opening pressure 32) is classic for TB, especially with positive GeneXpert pending. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Give IV aciclovir 10 mg per kg 8 hourly for possible herpes encephalitis and await MRI brain imaging
options.rationale: HSV encephalitis produces temporal lobe changes and PCR-positive CSF, not basal meningeal enhancement with markedly low glucose; aciclovir alone misses the treatable TB. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Start RIPE anti-tubercular therapy alone without corticosteroids because steroids risk TB dissemination
options.rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TB meningitis and is standard alongside RIPE; withholding steroids loses a proven mortality benefit. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

options.text: Start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol plus IV dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day tapered over 8 weeks
options.rationale: TB meningitis is treated with standard RIPE quadruple therapy plus adjunctive dexamethasone (Thwaites regimen), which reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults. (Source: WHO TB Consolidated Guidelines)

explanation.summary: TB meningitis is treated with a 2 month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, then a 7 to 10 month continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid, alongside adjunctive dexamethasone tapered over 6 to 8 weeks. Steroids reduce mortality by around 30 percent. CSF classically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, very low glucose, and high opening pressure. GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is the first-line rapid test.
key_points: TBM treatment: 2 months RIPE plus 7 to 10 months RH, with dexamethasone taper
Dexamethasone reduces mortality across HIV-negative and HIV-positive adults
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, protein over 1 g/L, glucose under 40% serum
GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra on CSF is preferred rapid diagnostic
explanation.pearls: Thwaites steroid regimen: dexamethasone 0.4 mg per kg per day IV for 1 week, 0.3 for week 2, 0.2 for week 3, 0.1 for week 4, then 4 mg orally reducing over 4 weeks; add pyridoxine 25 mg daily with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy.
